title: Eikev: not my hand alone (Deuteronomy 8:17–18)
hookLine: beware saying "my power and the might of my hand" earned this

cards: A founder at a podcast microphone tells the success story. I started in a garage. I worked eighteen-hour days.

Nobody believed in me. It's often true. But the parents who covered rent, the teacher who noticed, the lucky timing, the country with roads and courts, the health that held: they often get edited out.
Not out of malice. Success tends to tell itself in the first person. Moses saw this coming for a people about to move from tents into houses.
In the middle of Eikev he warns them about one sentence they'll be tempted to say.

teach.b: The chapter starts with gratitude. In the old Jewish translation: "And thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God for the good land which He hath given thee."
That verse is the root of the Jewish grace after meals, birkat hamazon. You eat, you're full, you bless. Then, right away, the warning.
When you've eaten and are full, Moses says, and built fine houses, and your herds and silver and gold have multiplied, watch out that your heart doesn't lift itself up and forget.
And the sentence: "and thou say in thy heart: 'My power and the might of my hand hath gotten me this wealth.'" In Hebrew, kochi v'otzem yadi. My strength, and the might of my hand.

Then the answer: "But thou shalt remember the LORD thy God, for it is He that giveth thee power to get wealth." Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say you did nothing, or that work is pointless.
Your hand was real. It says the power in the hand came from somewhere. Strength, health, wits, the land itself: in the verse's telling, given.
The danger isn't wealth. It's the sentence, said in your heart, that erases everyone and everything that made the wealth possible. And notice the timing.
Not in hunger. The warning comes when you're full. The same full stomach that leads to a blessing can lead to forgetting, and Moses puts the two side by side, a few verses apart.

how: Jews say birkat hamazon, the grace after meals, after eating bread, based on Deuteronomy 8:10, and some teachers pair it with the warning a few verses later against saying my power and the might of my hand.

o: wealth: the riches of the new land
pride: the heart that lifts itself

p: my power and the might of my hand
that giveth thee power to get wealth

s: the verse says hard work is pointless
your hand was real; the power in it was given.
the grace after meals comes from this chapter
Deuteronomy 8:10: eat, be satisfied, and bless.
Moses warns about this sentence while the people are hungry
he warns about it for when they've eaten, built houses and grown rich.

games.q: you've built a fine house and your wealth has grown. what sentence does Moses warn you not to say in your heart?
o: my power and the might of my hand got me this.
I am grateful for what I've been given.
I should share some of this.
games.why: kochi v'otzem yadi. the answer: remember who gives you the power to get wealth.

practice: Think of one thing you're proud of, and tell its story to yourself in one sentence, the way you would at a party.
Now tell it again, slowly, and let the hidden helpers in: who paid, taught, waited, believed you, and what luck you had. Let your thanks rest on one of them.
